hints: Compare what the leaves are doing in the day versus the night, and ask yourself when water loss by transpiration and upward movement in the xylem will be fastest.
Remember the difference between cohesion (water to water) and adhesion (water to wall), and how a fast-moving water column creates tension, which is a pull or negative pressure, inside the xylem.
walkthrough:
**Connect Time of Day to Transpiration**

Think like the tree. In the day it is warm, bright and stomata are open, so transpiration is high. At night stomata close and transpiration is very low.

So ask: when is the pull of water up the xylem strongest?

**Apply the Cohesion-Tension Theory**

In the day, rapid evaporation from leaves pulls the continuous column of water molecules upwards. Because water molecules stick together by cohesion, this creates tension in the column.

Tension means the water is under negative pressure, so the pressure inside the xylem vessels falls.

**Explain the Change in Diameter**

When pressure inside falls during the day, the slightly elastic lignified walls of the xylem are drawn inwards a little, so the whole stem diameter decreases. At night, transpiration stops, tension is released, pressure returns to normal and the walls spring back outwards.

That matches option B exactly.

options.A: This mixes up terms. Cohesion is water to water, not water to lignin (that is adhesion), and it is tension, not cohesion itself, that lowers pressure and pulls walls in.
options.B: Correct. High daytime transpiration creates tension in the moving water column, lowering pressure inside xylem vessels so their elastic walls move inwards and stem diameter falls.
options.C: Adhesion is attraction of water to the wall, but it does not push walls outwards. At night the diameter increases because daytime tension is released, not because of an outward push.
options.D: This confuses vocabulary. Water molecules sticking to one another is cohesion, not adhesion, and at night there is no increased positive pressure pushing out, only relaxation of daytime tension.
